Set working directory (containing fastq data)
```{r, message = FALSE}
setwd("") ### <- */fastq
# getwd()
```

Since dada2 is available as part of the Bioconductor Project Package Repository, install/load BiocManager (BioConductor)
```{r setup, include=FALSE}
#install.packages("BiocManager")
library(BiocManager)
# packageVersion("BiocManager")
# ‘1.30.26’
```

Install/load dada2 via BiocManager
```{r setup, echo = FALSE}
# BiocManager::install("dada2", version = "3.21", force = TRUE)
library(dada2)
# packageVersion("dada2")
# 1.36.0’
```

To use the dada2 pipeline, primers must be removed from the amplicon sequence data. To do this, the 'cutadapt' tool is used, which can be installed as a conda package. Miniconda can be installed here:
https://www.anaconda.com/docs/getting-started/miniconda/main

One installed, run the following command in Terminal:
conda install -c bioconda cutadapt

Once conda has been installed, install/load remaining required packages
```{r, message = FALSE}
# BiocManager::install("DECIPHER")
library(DECIPHER)
# packageVersion("DECIPHER")
# ‘3.4.0’

library(ShortRead)
# packageVersion("ShortRead")
# ‘1.66.0’

library(Biostrings)
# packageVersion("Biostrings")
# ‘2.76.0’

library(ggplot2)
# packageVersion("ggplot2")
# ‘3.5.2’

library(stringr) # not strictly required but useful
# packageVersion("stringr")
# ‘1.5.1’

library(readr)
# packageVersion("readr")
# 2.1.5’

# library
library(phyloseq)
# packageVersion("phyloseq")
# ‘1.52.0’
```

Set a seed for reproducibility. This initializes R’s random number generator to a specific state defined by the number (the seed). This ensures anyone who uses your code with the same seed will get the same results
```{r}
set.seed(106)
```

The dada2 pipeline is intended to be used with demultiplexed, paired-end fastq files. That is to say, the samples must be separated into individual files and ordered such that forward and reverse reads of the same sample are matched. 

The pattern of the filenames should be the same for all forward and reverse files. In this example, the names are formatted as such: 

*samplename*_R1_001.fastq.gz         for forward reads 
*samplename*_R2_001.fastq.gz         for reverse reads

Define the path of sequences to be processed
```{r}
path <- "" ### <- */fastq
```

Then create a vector of file names, one for the forward reads and one for the reverse. The samples vector contains our sample names, extracted from the file names using a regular expression. For Illumina data, often the sample name is everything before the first underscore.
```{r}
# filter and store only fastq.gz files
fwd_files <- sort(list.files(
  path,
  pattern = "_R1_001\\.fastq\\.gz$",
  full.names = TRUE
))

rev_files <- sort(list.files(
  path,
  pattern = "_R2_001\\.fastq\\.gz$",
  full.names = TRUE
))
```

Can also be useful to have a vector of just sample names (which, in this case, is everything up until the first underscore)
```{r}
samples = str_extract(basename(fwd_files), "^[^_]+")
names(fwd_files) <- samples
names(rev_files) <- samples
```

Define primer sequences to be clipped off all reads. The forward primer will be at the beginning of the forward read and the reverse primer will be at the beginning of the reverse read. The reverse complements are included in case the amplicon sequence is shorter than our read length. When this happens the sequence will contain the reverse complement of the opposite primer, i.e. there may be reverse-complemented reverse primer at the end of the forward read.
```{r}
fwd_primer <- "ACGTCTGGTTCAGGGTTGTT"
rev_primer <- "TTAGTTTCTTTTCCTCCGCT"

fwd_primer_rev <- as.character(reverseComplement(DNAStringSet(fwd_primer)))
rev_primer_rev <- as.character(reverseComplement(DNAStringSet(rev_primer)))
```

To ensure we have the right primers, and the correct orientation of the primers on the reads, we will verify the presence and orientation of these primers in the data.
```{r}
all_orients <- function(primer) {
    # Create all orientations of the input sequence
    require(Biostrings)
    dna <- DNAString(primer)  # The Biostrings works w/ DNAString objects rather than character vectors
    orients <- c(fwd_primer = dna, 
                 fwd_primer_complement = Biostrings::complement(dna), 
                 rev_primer = Biostrings::reverse(dna), 
                 rev_primer_complement = Biostrings::reverseComplement(dna))
    return(sapply(orients, toString))  # Convert back to character vector
}

fwd_primer_orients <- all_orients(fwd_primer)
rev_primer_orients <- all_orients(rev_primer)

fwd_primer_orients
```
            fwd_primer  fwd_primer_complement             rev_primer  rev_primer_complement 
"ACGTCTGGTTCAGGGTTGTT" "TGCAGACCAAGTCCCAACAA" "TTGTTGGGACTTGGTCTGCA" "AACAACCCTGAACCAGACGT" 

The presence of ambiguous bases (Ns) in the sequencing reads makes accurate mapping of short primer sequences difficult. Next we are going to “pre-filter” the sequences just to remove those with Ns, but perform no other filtering.
```{r}
fwd_files_filtN <- file.path(path, "filtN", basename(fwd_files))
rev_files_filtN <- file.path(path, "filtN", basename(rev_files))
filterAndTrim(fwd_files, fwd_files_filtN, rev_files, rev_files_filtN, maxN = 0, multithread = TRUE)
```

We can now count the number of times the primers appear in the forward and reverse read, while considering all possible primer orientations. 

Identifying and counting the primers on one set of paired end FASTQ files is sufficient, assuming all the files were created using the same library preparation, so we’ll just process the first sample.
```{r}
primer_hits <- function(primer, fn) {
    # counts number of reads in which the primer is found
    nhits <- vcountPattern(primer, sread(readFastq(fn)), fixed = FALSE)
    return(sum(nhits > 0))
}

rbind(FW_in_forward_reads = sapply(fwd_primer_orients, primer_hits, fn = fwd_files_filtN[[1]]), 
      FW_in_reverse_reads = sapply(fwd_primer_orients, primer_hits, fn = rev_files_filtN[[1]]), 
      RV_in_forward_reads = sapply(rev_primer_orients, primer_hits, fn = fwd_files_filtN[[1]]), 
      RV_in_reverse_reads = sapply(rev_primer_orients, primer_hits, fn = rev_files_filtN[[1]]))
```
                    fwd_primer fwd_primer_complement rev_primer rev_primer_complement
FW_in_forward_reads     107983                     0          0                     2
FW_in_reverse_reads          2                     0          0                    14
RV_in_forward_reads          0                     0          0                    26
RV_in_reverse_reads     106171                     0          0                     0

As expected, the FW primer is found in the forward reads in its forward orientation, and in some of the reverse reads in its reverse-complement orientation (due to read-through when the ITS region is short). Similarly the RV primer is found with its expected orientations.

Note: Orientation mixups are a common trip-up. If, for example, the RV primer is matching the reverse reads in its rev_primer_complement orientation, then replace RV with its reverse-complement orientation (REV <- REV.orient[["RevComp"]]) before proceeding.

Remove primers using 'cutadapt', and check that they have been successfully removed. Cutadapt was designed to remove sequencing adapters that sometimes get left on reads after sequencing, however, it’s main function is to detect and trim off regions that match a known sequence, which is precisely what we want to do here.

Cutadapt is best installed using conda and can also be used directly from the command line. Here, however, we will run cutadapt in RStudio using the 'system2' command. The first parameter to system2 is the program we wish to run and the second is character vector of arguments and their values
```{r}
cutadapt <- path.expand("/opt/miniconda3/envs/cutadapt_env/bin/cutadapt")
# check installed correctly
system2(cutadapt, args = "--version")
# 5.2
```

We now create output filenames for the cutadapt-ed files, and define the parameters we are going to give the cutadapt command. The critical parameters are the primers, and they need to be in the right orientation, i.e. the FW primer should have been matching the forward-reads in its forward orientation, and the RV primer should have been matching the reverse-reads in its forward orientation. 

Briefly:
-g: sequence to trim off the 5’ end of the forward read (the forward primer)
-a: sequence to trim off the 3’ end of the forward read (the reverse complemented reverse primer)
-G: sequence to trim off the 5’ end of the reverse read (the reverse primer)
-A: sequence to trim off the 3’ end of the reverse read (the reverse complemented forward primer)

In addition, add '-m 50' to get rid of very short or 'junk' (low-quality) reads, '--max-n 1' to get rid of reads that have any N’s in them (ambiguous base calls), and -n 2 so that cutadapt will remove multiple primer hits if there happens to be read-through. '--discard-untrimmed' is also added so only reads that contain a primer will be kept ensuring we keep only valid amplicons. And finally, a '-q 15' will trim off low quality bases from the 3’ end.

This small amount of trimming can remove the need for truncating the reads later on but this is something that may vary from run to run it and an important paramter to consider for your own data

Create an output directory to store the clipped files
```{r}
cut_dir <- file.path(path, "cutadapt")

if (!dir.exists(cut_dir)) dir.create(cut_dir)

fwd_cut <- file.path(cut_dir, basename(fwd_files))
rev_cut <- file.path(cut_dir, basename(rev_files))

# add names
names(fwd_cut) <- samples
names(rev_cut) <- samples
```

It's good practice to keep some log files so let's create some file names that we can use for those 
```{r}
cut_logs <- path.expand(file.path(cut_dir, paste0(samples, ".log")))

cutadapt_args <- c("-g", fwd_primer, 
                   "-a", rev_primer_rev, 
                   "-G", rev_primer, 
                   "-A", fwd_primer_rev,
                   "-n", 2, 
                   "--discard-untrimmed")
```

Loop over the list of files, running cutadapt on each file
```{r}
for (i in seq_along(fwd_files)) {
  system2(cutadapt, 
          args = c(cutadapt_args,
                   "-o", fwd_cut[i], 
                   "-p", rev_cut[i], 
                   fwd_files[i], 
                   rev_files[i]),
                   stdout = cut_logs[i])  
}

# check
head(list.files(cut_dir))
```

As a sanity check, we can count the presence of primers in the first cutadapt-ed sample:
```{r}
rbind(FW_in_forward_reads = sapply(fwd_primer_orients, primer_hits, fn = fwd_cut[[1]]), 
      FW_in_reverse_reads = sapply(fwd_primer_orients, primer_hits, fn = rev_cut[[1]]), 
      RV_in_forward_reads = sapply(rev_primer_orients, primer_hits, fn = fwd_cut[[1]]), 
      RV_in_reverse_reads = sapply(rev_primer_orients, primer_hits, fn = rev_cut[[1]]))
```
                    fwd_primer fwd_primer_complement rev_primer rev_primer_complement
FW_in_forward_reads          0                     0          0                     0
FW_in_reverse_reads          0                     0          0                     0
RV_in_forward_reads          0                     0          0                     0
RV_in_reverse_reads          0                     0          0                     0

The primer-free sequence files are now ready to be analysed using the dada2 pipeline. Similar to the earlier steps of reading in FASTQ files, we read in the names of the cutadapt-ed FASTQ files and applying some string manipulation to get the matched lists of forward and reverse fastq files.
```{r}
# Forward and reverse fastq filenames have the format:
FW_cut <- sort(list.files(cut_dir, pattern = "R1", full.names = TRUE))
RV_cut <- sort(list.files(cut_dir, pattern = "R2", full.names = TRUE))

# Extract sample names, assuming filenames have format:
sample_names <- function(fname) strsplit(basename(fname), "_")[[1]][1]
sample_names <- unname(sapply(FW_cut, sample_names))
head(sample_names)
```

We now inspect read quality profiles
```{r}
plotQualityProfile(FW_cut[1:3])
plotQualityProfile(RV_cut[1:3])
```

The quality profile plot is a gray-scale heatmap of the frequency of each quality score at each base position. The median quality score at each position is shown by the green line, and the quartiles of the quality score distribution by the orange lines. The red line shows the scaled proportion of reads that extend to at least that position.

The forward reads are of good quality. The red line shows that a significant chunk of reads were cutadapt-ed to about XXXnts in length, likely reflecting the length of the amplified ITS region in one of the taxa present in these samples. Note that, unlike in a bacterial 16S workflow, we will not be truncating the reads to a fixed length, as the ITS region has significant biological length variation that is lost by such an appraoch.



We now filter and trim the reads
```{r}
# Create an output directory to store the filtered files
filt_dir <- file.path(path, "filtered")
if (!dir.exists(filt_dir)) dir.create(filt_dir)

fwd_filt <- file.path(filt_dir, basename(fwd_files))
rev_filt <- file.path(filt_dir, basename(rev_files))
```

We will use standard filtering paraments: 
  maxN = 0 (DADA2 requires sequences contain no Ns), 
  truncQ = 2, 
  rm.phix = TRUE,
  maxEE=2. 
  
The maxEE parameter sets the maximum number of “expected errors” allowed in a read, which is a better filter than simply averaging quality scores
Note: We enforce a minLen here, to get rid of spurious very low-length sequences. This was not needed in the 16S Tutorial Workflow because truncLen already served that purpose.
```{r}
filtered_out <- filterAndTrim(FW_cut, 
                              fwd_filt, 
                              RV_cut, 
                              rev_filt, 
                              maxN = 0, 
                              maxEE = c(2, 2), 
                              truncQ = 2,
                              minLen = 50, 
                              rm.phix = TRUE, 
                              compress = TRUE, 
                              multithread = TRUE)  # on windows, set multithread = FALSE

head(filtered_out)
```

Now we need to learn errors. Dada2 learns the error profile for your data using an interative approach. These error profiles are used in the next step to correct errors.
```{r}
# Forward
err_fwd <- learnErrors(fwd_filt, multithread = TRUE)
# 101129273 total bases in 361782 reads from 3 samples will be used for learning the error rates.

# Reverse
err_rev <- learnErrors(rev_filt, multithread = TRUE)
# 101124020 total bases in 361782 reads from 3 samples will be used for learning the error rates.

# Plot errors to visualise
plotErrors(err_fwd, nominalQ = TRUE)
plotErrors(err_rev, nominalQ = TRUE)
# The plot shows how well the estimated error rates fit the observed rates. The black line should line up reasonably well with the black points. This looks reasonable so we continue on.
```

At this step, the core sample inference algorithm is applied to the dereplicated data. See: https://www.nature.com/articles/nmeth.3869#methods
This deionises (aka error-corrects) the sequences
```{r}
# Forward
dada_fwd <- dada(fwd_filt, err = err_fwd, multithread = TRUE)
# Check
dada_fwd

# Reverse
dada_rev <- dada(rev_filt, err = err_rev, multithread = TRUE)
# Check
dada_rev
```

Now that we have accurate sequences we can merge the paired-end reads to reconstruct the full amplicon 

Note that most sequences should succesfully overlap, unless your trimming parameters were too aggresive (i.e. too much sequence was trimmed off the end) or you have amplicons that are longer than the combined read length (>500 bp, in this case). In the latter case these reads can still be used but will need special handling (more details to come on those cases).
```{r}
mergers <- mergePairs(dadaF = dada_fwd,
                      dadaR = dada_rev,
                      derepF = fwd_filt,
                      derepR = rev_filt,
                      maxMismatch = 1, 
                      verbose=TRUE)
```

Construct an amplicon sequence variant (ASV) table (a higher-resolution version of the OTU table produced by traditional methods)
```{r}
seqtab <- makeSequenceTable(mergers)
dim(seqtab)
# [1] 81 1113
```

Remove chimeras (don’t worry if a lot of sequences are discarded - the number of chimeras varies but can be quite high in some cases)

Note: A chimera (or chimeric sequence) refers to a DNA sequence that is artificially formed by the erroneous joining of two or more sequences from different origins—usually during sample preparation or sequencing processes. These sequences do not represent real biological molecules, and they can mislead downstream analysis if not properly identified and removed
```{r}
seqtab_nochim <- removeBimeraDenovo(seqtab, method = "consensus", multithread = TRUE, verbose = TRUE)
# Identified 907 bimeras out of 1265 input sequences.

dim(seqtab_nochim)
# 81 602
# 66 samples, 358 unique sequences)
```

Inspect distribution of sequence lengths
```{r}
table(nchar(getSequences(seqtab_nochim)))

# plot
hist(
     nchar(getSequences(seqtab_nochim)),
     breaks = 100
)
```

As expected, quite a bit of length variability in the the amplified ITS region.

Inspect the the number of reads that made it through each step in the pipeline to verify everything worked as expected. This is an important step, particularly if you’re trying to track down where something went wrong.
```{r}
# Use this small function to get the number of sequences
getN <- function(x) sum(getUniques(x))

track <- cbind(
  filtered_out, 
  sapply(dada_fwd, getN), 
  sapply(dada_rev, getN), 
  sapply(mergers, getN), 
  rowSums(seqtab_nochim)
)

colnames(track) <- c("raw", "filtered", "denoised_fwd", "denoised_rev", "merged", "no_chim")
rownames(track) <- samples
# Check
track
```

Assign taxonomy using IdTaxa

Now that we have a sequence table with the chimeras removed, we can classify/assign taxonomy to the sequence variants. Although there are multiple multiple taxonomic classification methods, we will be using IdTaxa, which is available through the DECIPHER package.


Training the classifier

The IDTAXA classification method relies on a training set that contains sequences that are representative of known taxa. Although there exists trained classifiers, we will be using the ITS2 Nematode database as our classifier. Since it is not trained, we will have to train the classifier using LearnTaxa, which is also available as a DECIPHER package. The train parameter of LearnTaxa contains the sequences included in the classifier as a DNAStringSet. Each sequence is formatted such that the names of each taxonomic level is separated by a semicolon. Once the sequence headers of the classifier are parsed, the taxonomy parameter will contain the taxonomic assignment, separated by a semicolon, for each sequence in train.

To use IdTaxa, we will need to convert the unique sequence variants that we want to classify into a DNAStringSet object. Now that we have our trained classifier (i.e. training set) and the sequences we want to classify, we can run IdTaxa. You can change various parameters of IdTaxa depending on your data. We recommend reviewing the [IdTaxa documentation] (https://rdrr.io/bioc/DECIPHER/man/IdTaxa.html) for further information. Here, we have specified several parameters:

- strand = "both" : by setting the strand parameter to “both”, each sequence variant is classified using both the forward and reverse complement orientation. The sequence varient will be classified as the result with the highest confidence.

- threshold = 60 : setting the threshold to 60 specifies when the taxonomic classifications are truncated. A lower threshold usually results in higher taxonomic level classifications, but lower accuracy (i.e. confidence). A higher threshold usually results in lower taxonomic level classifications, but with higher accuracy.

- bootstraps = 100 : this specifies the amount of times bootstrap replicates are performed for each sequence.

- processors = NULL : automatically uses all available processors.

- verbose = TRUE : displays progress.

- type = "extended" : by setting the type to “extended”, the output for each sequence variant will contain the taxonomic classification, the names of each taxonomic rank, and the confidence of the assignment.
```{r}
# BiocManager::install("DECIPHER")
# library(DECIPHER)
# packageVersion("DECIPHER")
# ‘3.4.0’

# Create a DNAStringSet from ASVs
dna <- DNAStringSet(getSequences(seqtab_nochim))

# Train the classifier
train <- readDNAStringSet("/Users/john.archer/Documents/Glasgow/anthelmogram/scripts/reference_databases/ITS2/Nematode_ITS2_1.0.0_idtaxa.fasta")
tax <- read_tsv("/Users/john.archer/Documents/Glasgow/anthelmogram/scripts/reference_databases/ITS2/Nematode_ITS2_1.0.0_idtaxa.tax")
training_set <- LearnTaxa(train, names(train), tax)

idtaxa <- IdTaxa(dna, 
                 training_set, 
                 strand = "both", 
                 threshold = 60, 
                 bootstraps = 100, 
                 processors = NULL, 
                 verbose = TRUE, 
                 type = "extended")

# Define ranks of interest
ranks <- c("domain", "phylum", "class", "order", "family", "genus", "species")

# Convert the output object of class "Taxa" to a matrix analogous to the output from assignTaxonomy
taxid <- t(sapply(idtaxa, function(x) {
          m <- match(ranks, x$rank)
          taxa <- x$taxon[m]
          taxa[startsWith(taxa, "unclassified_")] <- NA
          taxa
}))

colnames(taxid) <- ranks; rownames(taxid) <- getSequences(seqtab_nochim)

# Check
View(taxid)
```

```{r}
# Create a data.frame contaning sample names as rows and columns
samp_data <-  data.frame(
  row.names = samples,
  sample = samples
)

# Check
# View(samp_data)
# NOTE: To create a more detailed data.frame with additional variables as columns, see: https://benjjneb.github.io/dada2/tutorial.html

# Rename 'taxid' rownames as ASV names
asvs <- paste0("ASV_", 1:length(dna))
rownames(taxid) <- asvs
rownames(seqtab_nochim) <- samples
colnames(seqtab_nochim) <- asvs
names(dna) <- asvs

# Now we put everything into one phyloseq object (even the sequences) so it is easy to use
physeq = phyloseq(otu_table(seqtab_nochim, taxa_are_rows = FALSE),
                  tax_table(taxid),
                  sample_data(samp_data),
                  dna)

# Check
physeq
```
phyloseq-class experiment-level object
otu_table()   OTU Table:         [ 602 taxa and 81 samples ]
sample_data() Sample Data:       [ 81 samples by 1 sample variables ]
tax_table()   Taxonomy Table:    [ 602 taxa by 7 taxonomic ranks ]
refseq()      DNAStringSet:      [ 602 reference sequences ]


Plotting physeq data

Note: https://benjjneb.github.io/dada2/tutorial.html
There is a good example of how to anlalyse within-sample diversity (alpha diversity) across different variables. For example, you could perhaps plot diversity pre- and post- treatment in different cattle --- or perhaps plot bray-curtis dissimilarity between sites.

See: https://joey711.github.io/phyloseq/plot_bar-examples.html

Set ggplot2 theme
See: https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/ggtheme.html
```{r}
theme_set(theme_bw())
theme_set(theme_gray())
```


Basic plots 

The following is the default barplot when no parameters are given. The dataset is plotted with every sample mapped individually to the horizontal (x) axis, and abundance values mapped to the veritcal (y) axis. At each sample’s horizontal position, the abundance values for each OTU are stacked in order from greatest to least, separate by a thin horizontal line. As long as the parameters you choose to separate the data result in more than one OTU abundance value at the respective position in the plot, the values will be stacked in order as a means of displaying both the sum total value while still representing the individual OTU abundances.
```{r}
plot_bar(physeq)
```

Add fill color to represent the genus/species to which each OTU belongs.
```{r}
plot_bar(physeq, fill="genus")
plot_bar(physeq, fill="species")
```

Barplot of relative abundance
```{r}
top20 <- names(sort(taxa_sums(physeq), decreasing=TRUE))[1:20]
ps.top20 <- transform_sample_counts(physeq, function(OTU) OTU/sum(OTU))
ps.top20 <- prune_taxa(top20, ps.top20)
plot_bar(ps.top20, fill="species")

# Remove horrible black deviding lines:
plot_bar(ps.top20, fill="species") +
  geom_bar(stat="identity", position="stack", color=NA)
```
See: https://joey711.github.io/phyloseq/plot_bar-examples.html for more plot examples. 

Change order of samples along X axis
```{r}
# Check sample names
sample_names(ps.top20)

# change sample order
sample_order <- c(
  as.character(95:178),
  "PC1",
  "PC2",
  "PC3"
)

# View order
sample_order

# Make a new factor in the sample data
sample_data(ps.top20)$SampleID <- factor(sample_names(ps.top20),
                                         levels = sample_order)
plot <- 
    plot_bar(ps.top20, x = "SampleID", fill = "species") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Sample", y = "Abundance", fill = "Species") +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 270, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5)
  )


ggsave(
  filename = "AHG_illumina_01.png",
  plot = plot,
  width = 10,
  height = 6,
  dpi = 300
)

# Abundance is normalised (equalling 1) and *then* pruned (top 20) - meaning any taxa not in that top 20 are removed...
# Re-normalise after pruning:
re_norm_top20 <- prune_taxa(top20, physeq)
re_norm_top20 <- transform_sample_counts(re_norm_top20, function(x) x / sum(x))
plot_bar(re_norm_top20, fill = "species")
plot_bar(re_norm_top20, fill = "genus")
plot_top20_after_normalisation <- plot_bar(re_norm_top20, fill = "genus")
# Make a new factor in the sample data
sample_data(re_norm_top20)$SampleID <- factor(sample_names(re_norm_top20), levels = sample_order)

# plot
plot_AHG_illumina_01 <- 
  plot_bar(re_norm_top20, x = "SampleID", fill = "species") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Sample", y = "Abundance (%)", fill = "Species") +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 90,
      hjust = 1,
      vjust = 0.5
    )
  )
```

extract relative abundances of each species and store in spreadsheet
```{r}
# extract raw data
abund_table <- as.data.frame(otu_table(physeq))

# ensure samples are rows
if (taxa_are_rows(physeq)) {
  abund_table <- as.data.frame(t(abund_table))
}

# add species names
species_names <- as.character(tax_table(physeq)[, "species"])
species_names[is.na(species_names) | species_names == ""] <- "Unidentified"
colnames(abund_table) <- species_names

# add sample IDs
abund_table$Sample <- rownames(abund_table)

# compute sample totals (true counts)
count_matrix <- abund_table[, setdiff(colnames(abund_table), "Sample")]
sample_totals <- rowSums(count_matrix)

# convert to proportions (%)
abund_percent <- sweep(count_matrix, 1, sample_totals, "/") * 100
abund_percent <- round(abund_percent, 2)

# interleave output
out_table <- data.frame(Sample = abund_table$Sample)

for (sp in colnames(count_matrix)) {
  out_table[[paste0(sp, " (reads)")]] <- count_matrix[[sp]]
  out_table[[paste0(sp, " (%)")]] <- abund_percent[[sp]]
}

# write to .csv
write.csv(
  out_table,
  file = "AHG_illumina_01_ITS2_species_abundance.csv",
  row.names = FALSE,
  quote = FALSE
)
```
